title: Makar Sankranti (kites; the sun turns)
hook: a whole city on its rooftops, the sky full of kites, and an old warrior on a bed of arrows waiting for the sun to turn

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raksha Bandhan: lamp, tilak, thread, sweet, and your line, protection runs in every direction. Who did you tell you've got their back? Today, a festival that follows the sun. Day one hundred fifty-one.

In mid-January, go to Ahmedabad at sunrise and look up. Every rooftop in the old city has people on it. Families, grandparents on plastic chairs, kids with spools of string. And the sky is full of kites, paper diamonds in every color, tugging, dipping, fighting. Somebody's string cuts somebody else's, and a whole neighborhood yells the same word at once. Food comes up the stairs all day. By night there are paper lanterns floating up. It's called Uttarayan here. Elsewhere, the day is Makar Sankranti. And under all the noise, it's about the sun.
screen: `EVERY ROOFTOP FULL.` → `THOUSANDS OF KITES.` → `UNDER THE NOISE, THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Diwali, Holi and Shivaratri follow the moon, so their dates wander around the calendar from year to year. Makar Sankranti follows the sun, so it lands on almost the same day every year, in mid-January. Sankranti means crossing, the sun moving from one sign of the zodiac into the next. Makara is the sign we call Capricorn. So this is the day the sun crosses into Makara. It also marks the start of what the tradition calls uttarayana, the sun's northward journey, the half of the year when the days grow longer. And that turn matters in a famous story. In the Mahabharata, the great-uncle Bhishma falls in battle, shot with so many arrows that he lies on them like a bed, his body never touching the ground. He has a boon: he can choose the moment of his death. And he chooses to wait. For weeks he lies there, teaching, until the sun turns north, because uttarayana was held to be an auspicious time to leave the world. Only then does he let go. So why kites? People give different answers. It's a way of spending the whole day outdoors, in the winter sun, after the cold. Some say the kites are thanks sent up toward the sun. Some just say it's what this day looks like. The texts don't mention kites; the rooftops do. And there's something honest in that. A festival about the sun turning, and a whole city spends the day with its face turned up.
screen: `THE MOON WANDERS, THE SUN DOESN'T.` · `SANKRANTI: THE SUN CROSSES.` · `BHISHMA WAITS FOR THE TURN.` · `THE TEXTS DON'T MENTION KITES.` · then, large: `A WHOLE CITY, FACES TURNED UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: turn your face to the light. If you can, sit where there's a window or real daylight. If not, just picture winter sun on your face. Settle, and breathe. Tilt your chin up, just slightly, the way you would on a rooftop watching a kite. Feel the light on your forehead, your eyelids, your cheeks. The days are getting longer, or they will be. Breathe in, as if you could take in some of that warmth. Breathe out slowly. Let your shoulders drop, like a string going slack. The bell holds the time.
Makar Sankranti. The day the sun crosses into Makara, the start of its northward turn, kept with kites and a face turned up.
Your line: a face turned up. Today, step outside for five minutes of daylight, and look up. Day one hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: On Makar Sankranti, in mid-January, many Hindus bathe in rivers, give to those in need, share sweets of sesame and jaggery, and in Gujarat and elsewhere spend the day flying kites from rooftops to mark the sun's turn north.

original.note: Sanskrit: makara, the sign of Capricorn, and sankranti, the sun's crossing.

trapdoor: what you thought: a kite festival.
what it means: the day the sun crosses into Makara and begins its northward turn, kept outdoors with faces turned up.
what a scholar hears: a solar date in a mostly lunar calendar, and Bhishma waiting for uttarayana in the Mahabharata.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva and Anushasana Parva (Bhishma on the bed of arrows, waiting for uttarayana)
Makar Sankranti and Uttarayan (kite flying in Gujarat)

notes: Uttarayana: the tradition dates it from Makar Sankranti; astronomically the northward turn begins at the December solstice, and the sidereal date has drifted with precession. The script says 'what the tradition calls'. A Keeper may want the drift mentioned or not.
Bhishma's wait: roughly 58 nights in some counts; written as 'for weeks'. Confirm.
Explanations for kites are presented as 'people give different answers'; 'the texts don't mention kites' — confirm no classical source prescribes kite flying.
Ahmedabad setting; paper lanterns (tukkal) at night. Confirm.
